title: Establishing a quantitative link between crystal violet absorbance and biomass in biofilms
author: Stephens, Mahadevan, et al.

steps.title: Grow bacterial suspension
steps.instruction: Cultivate bacterial cells in suspended culture following the strain‑specific growth protocol.

steps.title: Prepare dilution series
steps.instruction: Prepare a dilution series for each sample using at least 23 mL per sample to cover an optical‑density range of approximately 0.1 to 2.0.

steps.title: Quantify planktonic cells
steps.instruction: Measure optical density of each dilution by two methods.

substeps.instruction: Measure 1 mL of each dilution in a spectrophotometer to obtain the OD value.
Measure 100 µL of each dilution in a microtiter plate reader (e.g., OD600 for E. coli).

steps.title: Determine dry cell weight
steps.instruction: Obtain dry cell weight (DCW) for each dilution by filtration and weighing.

substeps.instruction: Pre‑weigh a 0.2 µm filter paper or membrane.
Filter 20 mL of each diluted sample through the pre‑weighed membrane and dry to constant weight (air‑dry or oven‑dry).
Re‑weigh the dried membrane and subtract the initial mass to calculate DCW.

steps.title: Stain cells with crystal violet
steps.instruction: Perform crystal violet staining, washing, and extraction for absorbance measurement.

substeps.instruction: Transfer 1 mL of each dilution into a conical‑bottom Eppendorf tube.
Centrifuge the tube at 10,000 g to pellet the cells.
Decant the supernatant and wash the pellet with deionized water.
Repeat the centrifugation and decant step.
Add 250 µL of 0.1 % (w/v) crystal violet solution and resuspend the pellet.
Centrifuge again and decant the excess stain.
Gently wash the pellet by submerging it in a beaker of clean deionized water (avoiding spill) and decant into waste; repeat washes until the rinse water runs clear.
Add 375 µL of solvent (either 95 % ethanol or 10 % acetic acid) to each tube and resuspend the pellet to extract the bound crystal violet.
Centrifuge and transfer 100 µL of the resulting supernatant into a microtiter plate well.
Repeat the above washing, staining, and extraction steps for all samples.
Include blank wells containing all reagents except cells.
Measure absorbance of each well at 540 nm using a plate reader.

steps.title: Analyze and plot data
steps.instruction: Create calibration plots using the collected measurements, normalizing plate‑reader data to blanks.

substeps.instruction: Plot plate‑reader OD (540 nm) versus spectrophotometer OD (e.g., OD600 or OD660).
Plot spectrophotometer OD versus dry cell weight (g L⁻¹).

description: The original aim of this study was to develop a method of biofilm quantification that did not require the separation of a biofilm from its growth substrate through vortexing or scraping as most conventional methods require [15]. The theory was, if the baseline crystal violet absorption of the substrate was determined prior to any experimentation, we could determine an estimate for the cell count in the biofilm formation on said substrate at the endpoint of the experiment or by having numerous cultures running concurrently for sacrificial sampling on a time scale. However, our findings indicate that the accuracy of such estimates is highly dependent on the bacterial strain, owing to significant variability in the composition of EPS. The presence of various polysaccharides, for example, can give higher CV readings for a similar cell count [24]. As such, the direct application of this method for total biofilm biomass quantification is feasible only when validated for the specific organism in use. Despite this limitation for this specific use, this method provides a robust framework for normalization. Establishing a relationship between crystal violet absorbance and dry cell weight enhances the reproducibility of crystal violet-based assays and facilitates more consistent communication among researchers. Therefore, standardizing this quantification step will not only improve intra-laboratory data coherence but also enable meaningful inter-laboratory comparisons and collaborations. We, thus, advocate for routine inclusion of this normalization step in biofilm research protocols. This standardized approach enables more accurate estimation of biofilm-associated biomass and can support consistent evaluation of bioproduction metrics, ultimately improving the comparability of research findings across studies.
